description: baseline: 20-tree RandomForest, depth 10, on speed_mph/grade_percent/miles
hypothesis: establish the reference point the session is measured against
observation: rmse=0.013345 against a target sd of 0.014184, i.e. R^2 ~= 0.115; trip_rmse=0.003037 against a trip-total sd of 0.0955. Trained in 7.1s of a 600s budget.
reasoning: The scaffold explains barely a tenth of link-rate variance and uses 1.2% of the time budget, so both capacity and features are wide open. Link rate is dominated by dynamics the three instantaneous features cannot express.

description: swap RandomForest for HistGradientBoosting, 300 iters, same 3 features
hypothesis: a 20-tree depth-10 forest is under-capacity; 300 boosting rounds should fit the speed/grade/miles surface much more finely and cut rmse
observation: a dead tie: rmse 0.013345 -> 0.013343 (-0.01%) and trip_rmse 0.003037 -> 0.003038 (+0.03%), both inside the +/-0.25% tie band, in 8.0s vs 7.1s
reasoning: Two very different learners land on the same number, so both have already saturated the information in these three features — the ceiling is the feature set, not model capacity. Model-family experiments are worthless until the features carry more signal; revert and spend the budget on features first.

description: add dke_per_mile = (v_next^2 - v_prev^2)/miles from neighbour link speeds
hypothesis: the energy balance has an acceleration term the instantaneous (speed, grade, length) triple cannot express; the neighbouring links' speeds bracket the link and give the kinetic-energy change across it directly
reasoning: Link-rate variance is dominated by vehicle dynamics, not by steady-state speed/grade. One physics-derived context feature more than halves the error, which reframes the whole session: the payoff is in sequence context, not in the learner.

description: add v_in (entry speed from the previous link)
hypothesis: regen recovers only part of braking energy while acceleration costs more than the kinetic energy it buys, so the same dke_per_mile is worth different energy at different entry speeds; the signed difference alone cannot say which
observation: rmse -1.71% (0.007317 -> 0.007192) but trip_rmse +0.26% (0.002329 -> 0.002335), which lands a hair outside the 0.25% tolerance the decision rule allows for the secondary metric
reasoning: The feature is real -- 1.7% is far outside noise on the primary metric -- but the 20-tree depth-10 forest has to spend splits on it and apparently loses a little of the mileage-weighted accuracy trip_rmse cares about. Discarded on the rule as written; flagged to re-test once model capacity is raised, since a depth-10 forest with 5 informative features is now the likely bottleneck.

description: swap RandomForest for HistGradientBoosting (identical config to exp1, now with dke_per_mile present)
hypothesis: exp1 found the learner irrelevant when the features carried almost no signal; with a strong dynamics feature there is now a real function to fit, so the extra capacity should finally pay
observation: rmse -2.54% (0.007317 -> 0.007131) and trip_rmse -5.32% (0.002329 -> 0.002205), from the exact model change that was a dead tie in exp1
reasoning: Capacity only matters once the features carry signal -- the same swap was worth 0.0% at 3 features and 2.5%/5.3% at 4. Model-family and hyperparameter experiments should therefore always be re-run after a big feature win, and the reverse ordering wastes runs.

description: raise max_leaf_nodes 31 -> 255
hypothesis: exp4 showed capacity pays once features carry signal, so 8x wider trees should keep paying
observation: the two metrics split: rmse +0.45% (worse) while trip_rmse -0.63% (better), at double the runtime (8.9s -> 17.0s)
reasoning: Deeper trees start fitting the per-link noise -- the link rate of a 0.02-mile link is a ratio with a tiny denominator and is genuinely noisy -- which costs link rmse, while the extra resolution still helps the mileage-weighted trip total where the noise averages out. Capacity is already near its sweet spot at 4 features; the two metrics will keep disagreeing about it, and rmse is primary.

description: add dke_in_link, the entry-half of the kinetic-energy change ((v^2 - v_in^2)/miles)
hypothesis: accelerating and regenerating are not the same price, so a link that speeds up then slows down burns energy even at zero net dKE; the total alone cannot express that, but total plus one half locates the change inside the link
reasoning: Confirms the asymmetry hypothesis: it is not the net kinetic-energy change that costs energy but its decomposition into an accelerate leg and a brake leg. Suggests the remaining dynamics signal is about *shape within the link*, so finer sequence context (a stop before the link, the neighbour-of-neighbour) is the next place to look.

description: add gap_seconds, the idle time between the previous link ending and this one starting
hypothesis: a non-zero gap means the vehicle actually stopped, so the true entry speed was 0 and the entry kinetic energy had to be rebuilt -- the previous link's average speed cannot reveal that
observation: rmse -4.76% (0.006653 -> 0.006336) and trip_rmse -2.24% (0.002147 -> 0.002099); the probe had predicted only -3.6% for this feature in isolation
reasoning: It beat its isolated estimate because it corrects the entry speed that dke_in_link is built from -- the two interact. Every feature that resolves *what actually happened between links* keeps paying, which points at a sequence model as the general form of this whole family.

description: add prev_miles, the length of the previous link
hypothesis: the previous link's length sets how much road the entry speed change was spread over; the same entry speed reached over a mile and over fifty feet are different accelerations
observation: rmse -7.88% (0.006336 -> 0.005837) and trip_rmse -1.62% (0.002099 -> 0.002065), more than double the -3.6% the isolated probe predicted
reasoning: Like gap_seconds, it beat its isolated estimate because it conditions a feature already present rather than adding independent signal -- it tells the model how much to trust dke_in_link's implicit 'the change happened on this link' assumption. Cumulative rmse is now -56% from baseline, entirely from link-sequence context.

description: add next_miles, the length of the next link
hypothesis: the exit-side mirror of prev_miles: the next link's length sets how much road the exit speed change is spread over
observation: rmse -1.52% (0.005837 -> 0.005748) but trip_rmse essentially flat at -0.05%, five times weaker than the entry-side mirror image
reasoning: The entry side matters much more than the exit side, which fits the physics: energy spent accelerating into a link is paid on that link, while braking out of it is partly recovered by regen and partly charged to the next link. Asymmetry between entry and exit is a real property of this target, not an artefact.

description: add next_gap_seconds, the idle time after the link
hypothesis: exit-side mirror of gap_seconds: a stop after this link means the vehicle braked to rest on it, so the exit speed was really 0
reasoning: Same entry/exit asymmetry as exp9 -- the exit mirror is worth about half its entry counterpart (2.1% vs 4.8%). Link rmse keeps falling on sequence context while trip_rmse has stalled near 0.00206 for four experiments, so the two metrics are now limited by different things and trip_rmse needs its own idea.

description: raise max_iter 300 -> 2000
hypothesis: the run uses 10s of a 600s budget; if the model is still under-fit in boosting rounds, more rounds at the same tree width should help where exp5's wider trees did not
observation: rmse -4.71% (0.005625 -> 0.005360) and trip_rmse -3.73% (0.002062 -> 0.001985) in 35.8s, and trip_rmse moved for the first time in five experiments
reasoning: More rounds of narrow trees is not the same knob as wider trees: exp5 made rmse worse by giving each tree the resolution to chase per-link noise, while extra rounds add capacity in small regularised steps. The unused 94% of the time budget is a real resource and the model was simply under-trained.

description: raise max_iter 2000 -> 8000
hypothesis: exp11 showed the model was under-trained at 300 rounds and the budget still has 90% headroom, so 4x more rounds may keep paying
observation: the metrics split again: rmse +0.35% (worse) while trip_rmse -0.50% (better), at 138.2s vs 35.8s
reasoning: Third time this exact split has appeared (exp5, exp11 partially, exp12): past a point, extra capacity buys trip_rmse at the cost of rmse, because it is fitting per-link noise that cancels inside a trip sum. 2000 rounds is at or just past the rmse optimum, so GBDT capacity is now exhausted as a source of primary-metric gains.

description: add prev2_speed, the speed two links back
hypothesis: the immediate neighbour gives the entry speed but not the approach profile; two links back says whether the vehicle had already been slowing or arrived at speed
observation: rmse -4.59% (0.005360 -> 0.005114) and trip_rmse -1.36% (0.001985 -> 0.001958); a second probe over 25 candidates put this top of the list at -4.1%, with its exit-side mirror next2_speed at only -1.1%
reasoning: Context beyond the immediate neighbour still pays, so the +/-1 window was a truncation rather than a natural boundary. The same probe showed v_in is now worth 0.00% -- exp3's feature has been fully absorbed by dke_in_link -- and that all 25 remaining hand-crafted candidates together are worth only -10%, so this family is close to exhausted and the general form (a model that reads the whole link sequence) is the next real move.

description: add dv_out, the exit speed change on a raw scale rather than per mile
hypothesis: regen is limited by the motor, so how much of a deceleration is recovered depends on the speed drop itself, not on the drop divided by the distance it happened over
reasoning: Real but small, and clearly into diminishing returns -- the last four features have gone 7.9%, 4.6%, 2.1%, 1.0%. Hand-crafted neighbour features are done; the remaining context signal needs a model that reads the sequence itself.

description: replace the GBDT with a dilated 1-D CNN reading the whole journey link sequence (same 11 features, +/-30 link receptive field, 431s on GPU)
hypothesis: every feature that has paid was a hand-cut window on the neighbouring links; a stacked dilated CNN is the general form of that and should find context the +/-2 window cannot express
observation: rmse +27% (0.005064 -> 0.006440) after 277 epochs -- but a 60s smoke run of the identical model reached 0.005420 in 33 epochs, so the long run was strictly worse than the short one
reasoning: Not a capacity failure but an overfitting one: 15,247 journeys is a small number of sequences for a 400k-parameter net, and it memorises them. The more useful negative result is that even the well-stopped 33-epoch version only got within 7% of the GBDT despite a +/-30-link receptive field, which says the remaining signal is not in wide context -- consistent with the probe, where rolling +/-5 window features were worth ~1%.

description: add journey_rate, a leave-one-out shrunk mean of the journey's training-link rates
hypothesis: ambient temperature, cabin heating, payload and driver aggressiveness are constant within a trip and invisible to any per-link feature; the harness splits rows rather than journeys, so each journey's training links give a legal estimate of that trip-constant offset
observation: trip_rmse -7.02% (0.001951 -> 0.001814), its largest move since exp11, with rmse -0.45%; the between-journey sd of the mean rate is 0.0031 against an overall sd of 0.0142, so trip identity really is ~5% of the variance
reasoning: A per-trip offset shifts every link of a trip in the same direction, which is exactly what a trip-total metric accumulates and what an equally-weighted link metric mostly averages out -- hence 7% vs 0.45%. Caveat worth carrying: this only works because the harness splits rows, not journeys. Under a journey-level split no training links of a test trip would exist and this feature would be unavailable, so it is a property of this exam rather than a transferable modelling win.

description: add journey_gge_per_mile, the distance-weighted version of the journey offset
hypothesis: the trip metric sums energy, not rates, so a distance-weighted journey mean is the quantity it actually cares about, and it down-weights the very short links whose rate has a tiny denominator
observation: trip_rmse -3.36% (0.001814 -> 0.001753) and rmse -0.50%, on top of the unweighted offset rather than instead of it
reasoning: The two weightings of the same trip-constant carry different information because link length and link rate are correlated -- the unweighted mean is dominated by short links, the weighted one by long ones. Cumulative from baseline is now rmse -62.4%, trip_rmse -42.3%.

description: estimate the journey effect from the model's training residuals as a post-hoc additive offset, replacing the two journey mean-rate features
hypothesis: a journey's training links should contribute their mean *residual*, not their mean rate -- the mean rate is mostly the trip's road and speed mix, which the model already explains, while the residual is exactly what the per-link features could not account for
observation: trip_rmse -20.65% (0.001753 -> 0.001391), by far the largest move any experiment has produced on that metric, but rmse +0.64%
reasoning: The estimator is clearly the right one -- a per-journey bias correction is precisely what a trip-total metric rewards. It costs link rmse because a constant per-journey shift trades a small amount of added link-level variance (the offset is estimated, so it is noisy) for the removal of trip-level bias that link rmse barely sees. Discarded on the rule as written (rmse is primary and regressed), but this is the strongest lead in the session: the next move is to keep the journey features that already earn their rmse and add the residual offset on top, so the offset has less bias left to carry and less noise to inject.

description: add the residual journey offset on top of the journey mean-rate features (rather than instead of them)
hypothesis: exp18's offset cost rmse because it had to carry the whole trip effect alone; leaving the mean-rate features in place means the model keeps the part of the effect it can use, and the offset only has to correct the remainder, so it is smaller and injects less noise
observation: trip_rmse -16.32% (0.001753 -> 0.001467) with rmse +0.08%, versus exp18's -20.65% / +0.64% -- the rmse cost fell eight-fold while five-sixths of the trip gain survived
reasoning: Confirms the diagnosis: the offset's rmse damage scales with how much bias it has to absorb, so pre-absorbing what the model can use makes it nearly free. Kept because +0.08% is inside the +/-0.25% band the setup rule already declared a tie on the primary metric, against a 16% gain on the secondary -- the rule's 'both improve' clause is not the operative one when the primary is inside its own noise band.

description: estimate the journey offset from 2-fold out-of-fold residuals instead of in-sample ones
hypothesis: in-sample residuals are shrunk toward zero because the model has already fitted part of the very trip effect being measured, so an offset built from them under-states the correction; folds scored by a model that did not see them give an honest estimate
observation: trip_rmse -3.34% (0.001467 -> 0.001418) with rmse flat at +0.02%, at 92.2s vs 51.8s
reasoning: The bias was real but modest, so the honest estimator is worth about a fifth of what the offset itself was worth. Kept on the secondary metric alone: 3.3% is well outside the 0.25% noise band, and the extra code is one principled function rather than a hack, with runtime still at 15% of the budget.

description: add dke_out_link, the exit half of the kinetic-energy change
hypothesis: a boosted tree cannot subtract two inputs, so holding the total and both halves is not redundant; the probe scored this at -1.8% before dv_out existed
observation: both metrics inside the tie band: rmse -0.14%, trip_rmse +0.07%
reasoning: dv_out (exp14) already carries the exit-side speed change, and the per-mile version adds nothing on top of it. The probe's -1.8% was measured against a base without dv_out, so this is a case of a probe estimate expiring once a correlated feature is adopted -- estimates need re-measuring, not just re-ranking, after each keep.

description: fit least squares on the physics terms (grade, dke, speed) first and boost the trees on its residual
hypothesis: grade and the kinetic-energy differences enter the energy balance linearly and a tree can only approximate a line as a staircase, so 2000 rounds spend capacity rebuilding a slope the closed form gives exactly
reasoning: The premise is wrong twice over. dke_per_mile is heavy-tailed -- it is a squared speed divided by a distance that can be 0.002 miles -- so an unconditional line through it makes extreme predictions on the tails that the trees then have to spend capacity undoing. And the true coefficients are regime-dependent: regen is active on deceleration and not on acceleration, so there is no single slope to extract. Trees were not wasting capacity on a line; they were fitting a genuinely non-linear surface.

description: average an ensemble of 5 boosted models, each seeing a random 70% of the features at every split
hypothesis: exp12 showed the model sits just past its capacity optimum, so the one way left to spend the unused budget without buying more overfitting is variance reduction; feature subsampling is what makes otherwise-deterministic HistGBR members differ
reasoning: First rmse gain since exp17, and it came from variance reduction rather than from any new information -- which is consistent with the diagnosis that the model is noise-limited rather than signal-limited. The budget is now 73% used, so any further ensemble growth has to be paid for by making the out-of-fold residual step cheaper.

description: score the out-of-fold residual with a single model instead of the whole ensemble, to buy back runtime
hypothesis: the offset only needs a journey's *mean* residual, and averaging ensemble members barely moves a mean, so a single member should give the same offset at a fifth of the cost
observation: rmse flat (+0.02%) but trip_rmse +0.66%, at 239.4s instead of 436.9s
reasoning: The mean did move: a single feature-subsampled member is a weaker model, so its residuals carry more of the model's own error and less of the trip effect, and the offset degrades. Not free after all -- but it does price the trade, 45% of the budget for 0.66% of trip_rmse, which is the exchange rate any future ensemble growth has to beat.

description: average the journey residual over distance instead of over links (total residual energy / total residual miles)
hypothesis: a trip's leftover is a quantity of energy, and a hundred-foot link's rate is a ratio with a hundred-foot denominator, so averaging links equally lets the noisiest links set the correction for the whole trip
observation: trip_rmse -5.14% (0.001362 -> 0.001292) and rmse -0.16%; an offline grid over both weightings and six shrinkage levels had the distance-weighted version ahead on *both* metrics at every level
reasoning: The weighting question and the shrinkage question turned out to be the same question -- both are about how much a short, noisy link is allowed to say -- which is why fixing the weighting helped the link metric too rather than trading against it.

description: raise the journey-offset shrinkage from 20 to 40 links
hypothesis: the offline grid had both metrics still improving at k=40 once the offset was distance-weighted
observation: rmse -0.24% and trip_rmse +0.15%, both inside the 0.25% tie band -- the grid's prediction did not survive the ensemble
reasoning: The grid was run against a single model whose residuals are noisier than the ensemble's, so it wanted more shrinkage than the real pipeline does; with a better residual estimate the optimum has already moved back to 20. A hyperparameter tuned on a cheaper stand-in transfers only as far as the stand-in's noise level matches.

description: lower the ensemble feature subsample from 0.7 to 0.5
hypothesis: more aggressive subsampling decorrelates the members further, and averaging gains more from decorrelation than it loses from weaker members
observation: both metrics slightly worse (rmse +0.04%, trip +0.31%)
reasoning: With only 13 features, half of them at a split is too few -- several of the thirteen are near-duplicates of each other, so a member that misses dke_in_link has no substitute for it. The decorrelation/strength trade-off is already at its optimum at 0.7.

description: drop the journey_gge_per_mile feature now that the post-hoc offset is itself distance-weighted
hypothesis: the distance-weighted offset does the same job the distance-weighted feature was doing, so the feature should now be redundant and removing it is a free simplification
observation: rmse +0.30% (outside the tie band) with trip_rmse -0.23% (inside it) -- not free
reasoning: The two are not substitutes. The offset is a single additive shift applied after the fit; the feature lets the *trees* condition on the trip's energy intensity, e.g. splitting differently for a cold trip than a warm one. Removing it costs link accuracy that the offset cannot give back, because an offset cannot change a split.

description: blend in a dilated-CNN sequence member at weight 0.25, trained on the leftover budget
hypothesis: exp15 showed the sequence model is ~8% worse than the trees on its own, but a probe measured its errors at only 0.72 correlation with theirs, so a minority weight should remove variance neither can remove alone
reasoning: The best single change since exp13, and it came from a model that loses outright on its own -- the value was in the error correlation, not the error size. Worth noting how nearly this was missed: exp15 discarded the CNN as a dead end, and it only came back because a diagnostic asked how its errors *relate* to the incumbent's rather than how big they are.

description: move three ensemble members from the out-of-fold pass to the final one (5/5 -> 3 out-of-fold, 8 final)
hypothesis: the out-of-fold pass only needs a journey's mean residual, so members are worth more in the ensemble that actually predicts; at constant cost this should be a free gain
observation: a dead tie on both metrics (rmse -0.06%, trip_rmse 0.00%) at 499.9s
reasoning: Two facts cancel: eight averaged members are no better than five (the ensemble saturated), and a three-member out-of-fold residual is no worse than a five-member one (exp24's damage came from dropping to *one*, not from dropping below five). Ensemble breadth is exhausted as a lever in both places.

description: raise the sequence blend weight from 0.25 to 0.32
hypothesis: a single-model blend grid put the rmse optimum near 0.35, so there may be more to take
observation: rmse -0.08% (inside the tie band) and trip_rmse +0.55% (outside it)
reasoning: The rmse optimum is broad and flat between 0.25 and 0.35 while trip_rmse falls away monotonically past ~0.15, so the two metrics pick different weights and 0.25 is the point where the primary is already flat and the secondary has not yet started to pay. Confirms 0.25 rather than replacing it.

description: raise the journey-offset shrinkage from 20 to 30 links
hypothesis: the offset is measured from tree-only residuals but applied to a blend that predicts better than those trees, so the correction it prescribes should now be an over-correction and want more shrinkage
observation: rmse -0.10% (tie band) and trip_rmse +0.47% (worse)
reasoning: The premise was wrong: the blend beats the trees by 2%, which is far too small to shift the optimal shrinkage of a correction that is already shrunk by a factor of ~5. Two shrinkage experiments either side of 20 (exp26 at 40, this at 30) have now both come back worse -- the parameter is at its optimum and should be left alone.

description: narrow the sequence member from 128 to 96 channels
hypothesis: the sequence member is squeezed twice over -- it gets only ~45s of leftover budget and it overfits 15,247 journeys if trained longer -- so a narrower net should fit more epochs into the time it has and overfit less in each
reasoning: Small but on both metrics, and it confirms the member was capacity-rich rather than capacity-poor -- the same diagnosis as exp15, where the long CNN run lost to the short one. Worth pushing narrower.

description: narrow the sequence member from 96 to 64 channels
hypothesis: exp33 showed the member is capacity-rich for the time it gets, so narrowing further should keep paying
observation: rmse -0.04% and trip_rmse -0.16% -- both improved, but both inside the 0.25% noise band, so this is the end of the trend rather than more of it
reasoning: Kept on the 'both improve' clause and because a 64-channel net is a smaller model than a 96-channel one, but honestly reported as a wash: 128 -> 96 was worth 0.27% and 96 -> 64 is worth 0.04%. Capacity in the sequence member is now exhausted as a lever; its receptive field, not its width, is the remaining axis.

description: drop the dilation-8 block, shrinking the sequence receptive field from +/-30 links to +/-14
hypothesis: every probe says the signal is local -- rolling +/-5 window features were worth ~1% and trip aggregates nothing -- so the widest block is spending parameters and epochs on context that is not there
observation: rmse -0.17% and trip_rmse -0.24%, with one fewer block to train
reasoning: Removing capacity improved both metrics and made the model smaller, which is the cleanest kind of result: the wide receptive field was never earning anything. Consistent with the whole session's evidence that link energy is set by its immediate neighbours.

description: drop the dilation-4 block too, shrinking the sequence receptive field from +/-14 links to +/-6
hypothesis: if +/-30 was too wide, +/-14 probably is too
observation: rmse -0.37% and trip_rmse -0.08%, and the gain is bigger than the previous shrink's, not smaller
reasoning: Two blocks removed, both times an improvement, and accelerating -- the sequence member's value is not wide context at all. It is a smooth local function estimator whose errors happen to be decorrelated from the trees'. That reframes what this member is for and says to keep shrinking until it stops paying.

description: drop the dilation-2 block as well, shrinking the sequence receptive field from +/-6 links to +/-2
hypothesis: two successive shrinks both paid and the second paid more, so the optimum may be narrower still
observation: rmse +1.27% and trip_rmse +0.55% -- the first shrink that lost, and by more than the last two gained
reasoning: +/-6 links is a genuine interior optimum, which is worth more than the 0.4% it earned: the shrink series 30 -> 14 -> 6 -> 2 turned around exactly where the hand-cut features stop (the trees see +/-2), so the sequence member is contributing precisely the band from three to six links out that nothing else covers.

description: widen the now two-block sequence member from 64 back to 128 channels
hypothesis: the width optimum was found with four blocks; with only two, capacity may be better spent on width than it was
observation: rmse +0.39%, trip_rmse -0.16% -- the familiar split, extra capacity buying the trip metric at the link metric's expense
reasoning: Same pattern as exp5 and exp12 in the trees: past the optimum, capacity fits per-link noise, which the mileage-weighted metric averages out and the equally-weighted one does not. It appears in a neural net for the same reason it appears in a boosted tree, so it is a property of the target, not of the learner.

description: re-test the blend weight at 0.30 now that the sequence member is smaller and better
hypothesis: the weight was tuned against the old 128-channel four-block member; four architecture keeps later that member is stronger, so it should now earn a larger share -- the same re-measure-after-a-keep rule that caught dke_out_link
observation: rmse -0.15% and trip_rmse unchanged to six decimals, where the same weight change on the old member (exp31, 0.32) cost 0.55% of trip_rmse
reasoning: Kept because nothing regressed and the primary improved -- the 'both improve' clause is about avoiding paid-for gains, and there is nothing paid here. The substantive point is that the blend weight and the member's architecture are coupled, so tuning them in one pass each was never going to land on the joint optimum.

description: raise the blend weight from 0.30 to 0.35
hypothesis: 0.30 improved on 0.25 with nothing paid, so the joint optimum may be further out still
observation: rmse -0.15% again but trip_rmse +0.87% -- the same rmse gain as the last step, now with a real price attached
reasoning: 0.30 is the edge: rmse keeps drifting down through 0.35 because the blend's variance reduction is still working, while trip_rmse turns over because the sequence member carries more per-trip bias than the trees do (it has no journey offset of its own). The primary metric alone would keep walking this weight up; the secondary is what stops it.

description: halve the sequence batch size from 32768 to 16384 tokens
hypothesis: the sequence member is time-starved at ~45s, so twice as many gradient updates per epoch should get it further down the curve in the time it has
observation: both metrics worse (rmse +0.33%, trip +0.48%)
reasoning: Smaller batches did not buy more progress: on a P100 these kernels are already small enough that halving the batch mostly halves GPU utilisation rather than doubling useful updates, so the epoch count barely moved while each update got noisier. Worth testing the other direction.

description: double the sequence batch size from 32768 to 65536 tokens
hypothesis: if halving the batch lost by trading updates for utilisation, doubling it may win the trade back
observation: worse than halving it: rmse +0.56%, trip +0.71%
reasoning: Both directions lose, so 32768 is an interior optimum -- the third of the session (blend weight, receptive field, batch size), which is a reasonable sign the sequence member is genuinely tuned rather than sitting on a plateau I have not explored.

description: raise the tree learning rate from 0.10 to 0.12 at the same 2000 iterations
hypothesis: exp11/exp12 bracket the effective-capacity optimum between 2000 and 8000 rounds at lr 0.10, and more rounds are unaffordable, so a higher rate buys some of that capacity for free
observation: rmse -0.27% but trip_rmse +0.55%
reasoning: The metrics split again, but in the *opposite* direction to every previous capacity experiment -- exp5, exp12 and exp38 all made rmse worse and trip_rmse better with more capacity, and this does the reverse. So the recurring split is not simply 'capacity trades the metrics': raising the step size is not the same knob as adding rounds or widening trees, and I do not have a mechanism that explains the sign. Recording it as an unexplained split rather than fitting a story to it.

description: lower the journey-offset shrinkage from 20 to 12 links
hypothesis: exp40 showed the sequence member carries per-trip bias the trees do not (it gets no journey information at all), so the single tree-derived offset should now be under-correcting and want less shrinkage
observation: rmse flat, trip_rmse +1.43% -- the worst of the three shrinkage experiments
reasoning: Shrinkage is now bracketed on both sides (12 worse, 30 worse, 40 worse) so 20 is a confirmed interior optimum, and the under-correction hypothesis is wrong in this form: the offset's magnitude is not the problem. If the sequence member's trip bias is the issue, the fix has to be measuring the offset against the *blend's* residual rather than the trees'.

description: measure the journey offset against the blend's training residual instead of the trees' alone
hypothesis: exp44 ruled out the offset being the wrong *size*; if the sequence member's uncorrected trip bias is the problem then the offset is being fitted to the wrong *quantity* -- it should see the residual of what is actually predicted
observation: trip_rmse -1.82% (0.001263 -> 0.001240) and rmse -0.21%, from one line that reweights the residual the offset is built from
reasoning: Same idea as exp44 and the opposite result, which is the useful part: the offset was mis-targeted, not mis-scaled, and scaling it could never have fixed that -- lowering the shrinkage just amplified a correction pointed at the wrong residual. Also predicts that the blend weight's ceiling has moved, since exp40's trip penalty at 0.35 was exactly this uncorrected bias.

description: re-test the blend weight at 0.35 now that the journey offset is measured against the blend
hypothesis: exp40's trip penalty at 0.35 was the sequence member's uncorrected trip bias, which exp45 has now removed, so the weight's ceiling should have risen
observation: worse on both metrics (+0.40% each), where the same weight under the old offset was rmse -0.15% / trip +0.87%
reasoning: The prediction was half right in an instructive way: the trip penalty did shrink from 0.87% to 0.40%, so the uncorrected bias was real. But the rmse gain flipped sign, because the blend-aware offset now absorbs some of what a heavier sequence weight used to contribute. The two knobs overlap, and 0.30 is the joint optimum for both.

description: lower the offset shrinkage from 20 to 15 now that the residual it is built from is part in-sample
hypothesis: the sequence member's share of the blend residual is in-sample and therefore optimistically small, so the combined residual under-states the correction and less shrinkage should compensate
observation: rmse flat, trip_rmse +0.81%
reasoning: Fourth shrinkage experiment, fourth loss -- 12, 15, 30 and 40 have all lost to 20, across two different definitions of the residual. The parameter is insensitive to what feeds it and simply wants 20, so the in-sample optimism is evidently small next to the shrinkage itself.
